claims.overstatement: The claim says Greenfield et al. call faster progression in women one of the most reproducible findings. They do not, exactly. The Introduction's first sentence gives that label to women's heightened vulnerability to the adverse medical and social consequences of use. The next sentence states faster progression as established, for alcohol, opioid and cannabis dependence, citing six studies. Suggested wording: 'states it as established, beside calling women's vulnerability to adverse consequences one of the most reproducible findings'. Also, this review's list is alcohol, opioid (not split into prescription and heroin) and cannabis, with no cocaine and no heroin exception; the claim's list comes from McHugh et al. And this review does not call its evidence mostly treatment samples: one of the six sources is Dawson (1996), a general-population survey.
claims.note: Internal tension in the source. The Introduction cites Dawson (1996) for women advancing faster from use to first treatment. Section 2.3 describes the same study as finding no gender difference in treatment entry for 8 years after onset and men 13–20% more likely to enter treatment between 8 and 25 years. Section 2.3 also cites clinical studies for women's shorter interval from regular use to treatment entry, then says clinical studies found little difference in the likelihood or rate of treatment entry. The review was searched systematically (Medline and PsycInfo, 1975–September 2005) but the studies were not formally appraised, and the Introduction's progression statement gives no design, timing measure or adjustment.

claims.overstatement: The sentence that the dependence hazard ratios 'mostly reflect men's higher chance of ever becoming dependent, not faster progression' is the editors' inference, stated as fact. The authors read the same survival curves and a significant cohort x gender x time interaction (F = 54.08, p<0.01) the other way: men reached dependence faster than women, more so in recent cohorts. The inference fits Table 1 (similar mean times overall; 23.7% of men vs 16.2% of women who drank became dependent, my arithmetic), but the claim should label it as the editors' reading and report the authors' reading. Minor: the 38,309 are lifetime drinkers as the surveys define them (more than 12 drinks ever), not everyone who had ever drunk.
claims.note: Every Keyes number in the statement and magnitude checks: response rates 90% and 81%; n 53,238 (cohort ns sum to it); 38,309; 19.0 vs 17.8; gaps 3.0 and 0.4 (my subtraction); all ten hazard ratios and intervals; 5.6 vs 5.8 with ratio 1.04, not significant; 3.7 vs 4.2 with p = 0.02; 5.5 vs 6.4 not marked, and my t from the printed means and SEs is 2.40, which matches the card's approximation of about 2.4; 19.4 vs 23.5; and the totals 6.1 vs 7.0 really cannot be averages of the cohort rows (n-weighted row means about 14.8 and 13.2). Adjustment set: the Methods text says age was tested and dropped, but Table 2's footnote a, and the Results paragraph on the two-way interaction, list age among the controls. The claim follows the Methods text and should note the conflict or add age. The claim is right that the Discussion's statement that women were faster on neither step goes beyond Table 1 (cohort 2 dependence p = 0.02; cohort 5 treatment p = 0.002; total treatment marked p<0.05). Telescoping studies measured timing among people who reached each step, while the hazards here are among everyone at risk; the claim keeps the two apart correctly.

claims.overstatement: Two framing points. (1) 'The 1989 study that named telescoping': Marks & Clark say Lisansky first used 'telescoped development' in 1958, citing the 1952 WHO report, and that Piazza et al. are widely credited with defining the term in 1989. Better: 'the 1989 study usually credited with defining the term'. (2) The opening says the faster course was described in treatment and self-help samples. But the cannabis study Marks & Clark describe (Khan et al., 2013) is, by its title in their reference list, a NESARC analysis, that is, a national general-population survey. The claim calls it only 'a national sample'; it should say that this general-population study is described as finding the faster course for cannabis, second-hand and with its timing measure and adjustment not given.
claims.note: Every Marks number in the statement and magnitude checks against the running text: 1952 WHO report; 98 men, with 15 women's data excluded; 33 women and 105 men; 4.3 years; about 2 and 3 years later first drink and first intoxication; same age at treatment entry; Iowa 3,132 men and 395 women, about 2 vs 3 years after a first attempt to quit; Khan 1,217 women and 3,297 men, 2.5 years; 75 of 103; the term should be discarded. Randall et al. (1999) is listed by Marks & Clark among larger samples with fewer telescoping effects, while Keyes et al. (2010) cite it as clinical evidence of telescoping, so 'described in opposite ways' is right. The paper is a critical history-of-science analysis with no stated search or selection method. The 103/75 citation count comes from a Web of Science and PubMed search with no date or criteria given.

claims.overstatement: The 'difference from population surveys by who reaches treatment' is an earlier review's explanation (Becker, McClellan & Reed, 2017), which McHugh et al. adopt and put in terms of severity: women already in treatment probably have more severe disorders, and a subset of women may progress fast to severe disorders. The claim should attribute it. 'Mostly in treatment samples' is the review's own description, but the citation it gives for cannabis (Khan, Okuda, et al., 2013) is, by its reference title, a NESARC general-population analysis of alcohol dependence. So either the citation is a slip for the NESARC cannabis paper, or a general-population analysis is counted as a replication. Either way it sits uneasily with the review's statement that population surveys did not replicate telescoping.
claims.note: Substances confirmed: alcohol (Diehl 2007; Randall 1999), marijuana (Khan 2013; Lewis, Hoffman & Nixon 2014), cocaine (Haas & Peters 2000, drug-involved offenders) and prescription opioids (Lewis 2014); not heroin (Lewis 2014; Stoltman 2015, people not in treatment). Keyes 2010 is named as the population-based analysis that did not replicate. The review also states that women start use later (Keyes 2010; Greenfield 2010). It is a critical narrative review (search terms reused from Greenfield et al. 2007, 517 papers screened, no appraisal), and none of its telescoping studies are described with sample type, timing measure or adjustment.

claims.overstatement: The claim leaves out a qualification McHugh et al. give in the same paragraph: some evidence that women reach treatment more quickly after first use and after disorder onset (Alvanzo 2014; Blanco 2013; Lewis & Nixon 2014). That is time to treatment among people who got there, not a hazard among everyone at risk, so it does not contradict 'less likely, or slower'. But it should be reported next to the Keyes cohort-5 figure. The same paragraph says adolescent girls with alcohol use disorder were more likely than boys to receive treatment.
claims.note: All McHugh items in the claim check: 2015, women 10.4% vs men 11.1% of those needing treatment for an alcohol or drug use disorder received it (about 7.9 million women in need; CBHSQ 2016, which is NSDUH); under-treatment particularly notable among adult women with alcohol use disorder; for illicit drug use disorders, gender not associated with past-year treatment use (Compton 2007, a NESARC paper by its reference title). The paragraph also reports no gender difference in treatment entry for prescription opioid or cannabis use disorder in adults, and that men more often receive specialized treatment while women more often seek care in mental-health settings (Edlund 2012). All of it is second-hand and unappraised.

claims.overstatement: Three omissions make the claim's account slightly one-sided. (1) The small clinical retention studies split 5 to 2 against women: five found women more likely to drop out, two found men more likely. 'Disagreed in both directions' is true but hides that balance. (2) Kaskutas et al. (2005): the women-only day programme did no worse than the two community mixed-gender programmes. Only the hospital-based programme, which cost twice as much per week, had higher abstinence, and the review concludes women may be equally well served by good mixed-gender and women-only day programmes. (3) In the older-adult study, women still had fewer heavy-drinking days (none vs an average of four in the past month) after the abstinence difference disappeared.
claims.note: All Greenfield figures check: 280 articles 1975–2005; 11.8% randomized trials (plus 7.9% non-randomized or quasi-experimental and 31.2% prospective cohorts); 10,010 patients in 96 programmes (11 US cities), men 20% less likely to stay at least 90 days in outpatient drug-free care; 26,047 patients in 87 Los Angeles programmes, women more likely to complete where differences appeared; 4,689 adults (1,239 women; ADSS 1996–1999), gender not associated with completion after adjustment; older adults 79.3% vs 54% abstinent at 6 months, not significant after controlling for length of stay. 'Where a difference appeared it more often favoured women' is the review's own reading (section 4.1, 2nd paragraph, 14 citations; section 6, 4th paragraph). The randomized women-only vs mixed-gender comparisons are Condelli 2000 (no difference in early attrition), Strantz & Welch 1995 (higher retention in the women-only day programme) and Kaskutas 2005, the only one on substance outcomes. The switch to gender-specific groups is Bride 2001 (no change in completion or retention). The review notes that retention and completion were defined in many ways.

claims.overstatement: The claim says that where a difference appeared it more often favoured women. This review does not support that. Most of the differences it reports go against women: smoking-cessation outcomes worse in women, nicotine replacement working better in men, poorer response to disulfiram for cocaine dependence, worse outcomes with buspirone for cannabis and cocaine, and less often completed detoxification. Varenicline relative to other aids is the one difference favouring women, and naltrexone findings are mixed. The claim's summary of women-only and gender-specific treatment cites only the null rolling-group trial from this review. It leaves out the observational findings favouring women-only programmes (43 programmes, Niv & Hser 2007; criminal-justice outcomes; Orwin 2001), the randomized support for gender-specific treatment in subgroups of women, and the closed-group pilot in which the Women's Recovery Group did better. Disulfiram: the effect is unknown in women for alcohol use disorder; for cocaine dependence women responded worse.
claims.note: The McHugh numbers in the claim all check: COMBINE (n = 1,226, 31% women; the reference title confirms it is the COMBINE gender analysis, Greenfield et al. 2010); prescription-opioid trial (n = 653, 40% women; McHugh et al. 2013, the first author's own); 24 Clinical Trials Network trials (n > 11,000; Korte 2011), no retention difference; more than 1.7 million treatment episodes (Bornstein 2015), no completion difference except detoxification; women 1.2% in disulfiram trials (as an example, via Agabio 2016); the Women's Recovery Group as effective as mixed-gender counselling in the larger trial (Greenfield 2014). The review says most studies used substance use reduction or retention as outcomes and that many trials stratify randomization by gender but do not analyse by gender.

claims.overstatement: No material overstatement of this source; the claim is careful (association verb, no heritability, interaction confined to the probability scale, adoption-design limits stated). Minor wording points: (1) 'born in Sweden ... adopted within Sweden' is implied by the requirement of register data on a biological parent but not stated in those words; (2) 'a drug-related conviction' is broader than the paper's crime definition (Crime Register codes 5011 and 5012; convictions only for trafficking or possession, or only alcohol-related, were excluded); (3) 'adoptive siblings, who had no genes in common with the adoptee' would be more accurate as 'not biologically related to the adoptee' (biological siblings reared with the adoptee were excluded); (4) the 'about 0.15 percentage points' slope at the lowest biological-risk decile is a point estimate whose interval includes zero (environmental score with the interaction term: 0.0015, -0.0006 to 0.0036).
claims.note: Every Kendler number in the statement and magnitude checks against the source. Editors' calculation recomputed: with deciles coded 0-9 (Figure legend), slope of the environmental index = 0.0015 + 0.0005 x genetic decile = 0.0015 at decile 0 (0.15 percentage points) and 0.0060 at decile 9 (0.6 points): same as the claim. 820/18,115 = 4.53%; binomial 95% CI 4.22-4.83%, matching 4.2-4.8. 'Up to about 3 in 10 after age 5' = 100 - 70.9 = 29.1% (note 12,783/18,115 = 70.6%, slightly different from the paper's 70.9%). Sibling percentages: in Table 3 the proband is the adoptee and the relative is the sibling, so 10.7% vs 6.1% (full), 7.4% vs 5.3% (half) and 6.2% vs 3.2% (adoptive) are the siblings' own rates grouped by whether the adoptee has a record; the claim words them that way correctly. No heritability or variance-component estimate appears anywhere in the paper (the word occurs only in a cited title), so 'the study estimated no heritability percentage' is right. The paper's own Comment (5th paragraph) says its shared-environment finding is at variance with some adult twin studies whose shared-environment effects fade after adolescence, which supports the claim's parenthetical about the adoptive-sibling association.

claims.overstatement: None for the part attributed to this review: the claim labels it a narrative review, says 'without figures' and 'second-hand', and hedges the gene-environment point ('has been reported'). 'No longer detectable' renders the review's 'no longer a significant influence' fairly.
claims.note: Only the second-hand summary sentence and the last magnitude sentence cite this source, and both are supported. The review gives no twin heritability figure for any drug use disorder; the only twin variance figure it prints is for smoking abstinence (additive genetic influences 11%-74% of the variance, section 7), plus an unquantified 'highly heritable' nicotine-dependence phenotype (section 6), so the magnitude's wording ('for any drug use disorder') is exact. The review does not cite or discuss Kendler et al. (2012), the Swedish adoption study, anywhere in its text or reference list; its only 2012 Kendler citations are Dick & Kendler (2012a, 2012b), a review of gene-environment interaction in alcohol use disorders, cited without any heritability figure. So nothing in this source presents Kendler et al. (2012) as giving a heritability estimate.

claims.overstatement: None for this source. The claim is more cautious than the authors, who write that their analyses 'support a causal effect' (Discussion, 7th paragraph). Given non-shared confounding, exposure measurement error and the null within-MZ result for abuse or dependence symptoms, that caution is warranted. Minor wording: (1) the within-pair estimates are a little over a third of the weighted estimate (0.21/0.57 = 0.37; MZ 0.22/0.57 = 0.39), so 'about a third' slightly understates them; (2) the '29 childhood characteristics' were measured at the age-11 intake: 9 describe the twin, 20 the family and parents (parental substance use, psychopathology, education, income and others).
claims.note: Every number from this source in the statement and magnitude was checked against Methods › Participants, Tables 1A and 2A/2B, and matches: born 1977-1984; 1512 at intake (mean age 11.72); exposure self-reported at the age-14 follow-up (mean 14.8); outcomes at FU4 (mean 25.29). Weighted 0.57 (0.06); all pairs 0.21 (0.09); MZ 0.22 (0.10); DZ 0.20 (0.14). Abuse or dependence symptoms: weighted 0.36; all pairs 0.24 (0.11); MZ 0.17 (0.14); DZ 0.34 (0.16). Intoxication, all pairs 0.29 (0.15). 'Already differed beforehand, notably in delinquent behaviour and parents' drinking and smoking' matches Table 1A (standardized differences 0.51, 0.39 and 0.45; 13 of 29 covariates above 0.25). Editors' calculations from beta and SE (two-sided normal): all pairs p about 0.020, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.39; MZ p about 0.028, CI 0.02 to 0.42; MZ abuse or dependence symptoms p about 0.22, CI -0.10 to 0.44; intoxication all pairs p about 0.053. 'Remained' and 'not clearly associated' therefore hold without the printed p-values, which are not valid (see the p-value anchor). The caveat sentence is supported by the Discussion, 6th paragraph, and the co-twin Methods paragraph. Its example ('their own early use of tobacco or other drugs') is the editors' illustration, not the paper's, but it fits the paper: none of the 29 propensity covariates measures the twins' own substance use (Table 1A). Qualifiers the claim leaves out: zygosity did not significantly moderate any within-pair effect (Results › Estimated Effects, 2nd paragraph); the authors note that random exposure measurement error also shrinks within-pair estimates (Discussion, 4th paragraph); the exposure is 'by FU1' at mean age 14.8, not strictly by 14.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of this source. The claim is more cautious than the review's abstract, and its remark that the abstract's 'markedly attenuates or eliminates' is contradicted by the review's own Seattle 2012 summary is correct (Table 1; Results, 5th paragraph; Discussion, 7th paragraph). Two wording points: (1) 'more years with dependence' should be 'dependence at more of the follow-up interviews' (five interviews three years apart, 21 to 33, each asking about the past year); (2) the Young in Norway odds ratios of 1.5 and 1.6 were already adjusted for gender, not crude.
claims.note: Every number in the statement and magnitude that comes from this source was checked against Table 1 and the Results text and matches: n 522, 447, 808, 706, 1311; -3.465 and -13.828 (p<0.0001); OR 2.39 (1.10-5.20) and 5.75 (1.53-21.54), both against a first drink at 11 or older at a family gathering; -0.0631 (p>0.05); 0.3848 (p<0.0001); OR 1.68 (p<0.05, no interval); beta 0.44, then 0.53, 0.46, 0.45 and 0.46; OR 1.5 (1.2-1.9), 1.6 (1.3-2.1), and 1.2 (0.9-1.6) for both; search to 10 January 2013; five reports from four cohorts; no meta-analysis. One correction to the magnitude: 'no association with misuse or any dependence (ORs 0.96, 1.40 and 0.64 against a first drink at 11-14)' gives only the misuse odds ratios. The odds ratios for dependence at any follow-up were 1.49, 1.16 and 0.35 (all p>0.05; Table 1, Guttmannova 2011 row). Suggested: 'misuse ORs 0.96, 1.40 and 0.64, any dependence ORs 1.49, 1.16 and 0.35, all p>0.05, against 11-14'. Qualifiers the claim leaves out: the review warns that adjusting for peer variables may be overadjustment (Discussion, 3rd paragraph), which weakens attenuation as evidence of confounding; the Seattle 2011 sample was limited to people who started drinking before 21; the Rutgers sample was limited to people who completed every wave. The 'critically low' rating comes from the card, not from the source (confirmed in step 2).

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of note; if anything one understatement. (1) 'Did not reliably change a pretend money task' and 'neither ... reliably changed what they gave or took': with the drug-use description, readers took more money (punishment 62.05 vs 53.96 pence, Welch t(1557.96) = 2.81, p = .005, significant at the study's alpha of .01; d 0.14, interval 0.02 to 0.26), which the study's rule calls inconclusive only because the interval also reaches below its 0.20 bound; the paper's own Discussion makes the same simplification. Better: 'a small difference in money taken that the study could not show to be more than trivial'. (2) 'Large differences by the usual standard' fits d 0.87 and 0.95; 0.78 is just under Cohen's 0.8. (3) 'No personal or close-family history of substance use or psychiatric diagnoses' can be read as excluding anyone who had used drugs; the self-confirmed exclusion was of a substance use or psychiatric diagnosis in oneself or a known close relative. (4) 'A university participation scheme': the paper says research participation schemes (SONA), plural, across several institutions. (5) For the treatment framing, 'only inconclusive differences' is true of every self-report measure and of reward, but money taken (punishment) was equivalent (d -0.02), as the magnitude correctly says; the 'likely to succeed' version also said Alex was in a treatment programme rather than visiting a doctor.
claims.note: Every number in the statement and magnitude checks against the text and Table 1. Means: public stigma 50.59 vs 42.15 (RQ1), 49.62 vs 51.20 (RQ2); blame 8.61 vs 7.22 (RQ2); reward 248.11 vs 249.72 pence (RQ1). Directions on the means: drug use had lower social-distance scores (18.84 vs 23.76; lower = more distance), higher danger (17.37 vs 13.32) and lower blame (7.88 vs 8.81); the brain-disease label had higher social-distance scores (19.46 vs 18.38, i.e. less distance) and lower public stigma (49.62 vs 51.20), as the claim says; the uncertain (low-stability) framing had higher public stigma (52.15 vs 49.48), as the magnitude says. Recomputed from Table 1 means, SDs and ns: all 24 printed 'CI' intervals have the half-width of 98% intervals (z 2.326), none of 99% (z 2.576), e.g. social distance RQ1 98% 0.75-0.99 vs 99% 0.73-1.01, printed 0.74-0.99; this fits a TOST (1 - 2 alpha) interval labelled as 99%. Sample flow checks: 1,622 - 9 = 1,613; RQ1 1,613 - 53 = 1,560 = 819 + 741 (53 = 3.29%); RQ2 392 + 423 + 32 = 847 (3.78%); RQ3 362 + 383 + 102 = 847, so 102 is 12.04%, not the printed 11.96%. The vignette names no drug ('increasing drug use'), but the drug-use versions of four questionnaire items named opioid addiction (removed for the health-concern version), as the claim says.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of direction or causality. On imaging it says findings 'may mix effects', softer than the source's 'likely influencing'. Three phrases are inaccurate as worded and one is incomplete. (1) The simultaneous averages are described as use 'at the same time as cocaine or within a couple of hours'. That is the definition of only one source (Grant & Harford, 1990). The review defines simultaneous use as the same occasion with overlapping consumption or effects (Methods › 2.1, 1st paragraph). The pooled sources asked about co-administration at first use, in a session, ever in one session, use to come down from a cocaine high in the past 30 days, or use together in the past 12 months. Suggested: 'on the same occasion (definitions varied)'. (2) 'Single sources ranged from about a quarter to nearly everyone' holds for alcohol only. Simultaneous cannabis went down to 9.3% and 12.3% (Table 1), 12% in the text. (3) 'None excluded people who drink alcohol or use cannabis' leaves out that two of the 40 imaging studies excluded people who had used cannabis in the past week (3.3; Table 2, rows 9 and 20). (4) Incomplete: '(from the past 30 days to a lifetime)' also covered one urine-test source (Vanek) and one with no stated window (Schwingel). Where a source gave several windows, the shortest was used. No advice on amounts, timing, routes or combinations.
claims.note: Checked against the source, all of these match: 16 estimates = 11 from one PubMed search (January 1990 to June 2017) + 5 secondary analyses of US data sets; 10 US, 3 Canada, 2 Brazil, 1 Denmark; study years 1985-2017; all but one by self-report. Pooled 74% (50-89), 38% (20-60), 77% (62-87), 64% (47-79). I² 97-99%. Text ranges 24-98, 12-76, 37-96, 43-94 against Table 1's 23.5-87, 9.3-76.5, 34.9-96.5 and 43.2-93.7 (the magnitude is right that the fourth agrees). St Louis WTW and STOP (n 463 and 122, all women): to come down, alcohol 23.5% and 36.1%, cannabis 9.3% and 12.3%; past-30-day alcohol 79.5% and 71.3%. 40 imaging studies: 10 excluded alcohol dependence and 10 cannabis dependence (counted in Table 2). Animal studies: 2 of 40 gave alcohol (in utero, and adolescent alcohol before later cocaine), none cannabis. 75% vs 5% and 72.5% (= 29/40) vs 0%. Fisher's exact p recomputed at about 6e-11 and 9e-13 (stated p<0.0001). Tobacco: the authors write that nicotine with other substances, especially alcohol, may be more frequent than cocaine plus alcohol (Discussion, 4th paragraph). No appraisal of the sources is described. Figure 1 was not viewable, and the text does not give how many sources entered each average. Editors' check by DerSimonian-Laird logit pooling of the Table 1 values, using the review's rules (shortest window, powder over crack): it reproduces simultaneous cannabis, 37.9% (19.7-60.3) from 7 sources, and concurrent alcohol, 77.0% (62.1-87.2) from 11 sources, exactly. It gives 70.1% (46.1-86.5) for simultaneous alcohol (8 sources) and 66.5% (49.5-80.1) for concurrent cannabis (8 sources), against the printed 74% and 64%, so the inputs to those two cannot be identified from Table 1. 'Certainty' and 'Status' are not judged here; the 'critically low' rating is from the card (confirmed in step 2).

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E is high overall, driven by confounding and the ecological moderator. The response-rate facts check out: below 60% in five countries; non-response 12.3% to 54.1%.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Minor' is defensible because the abstract and Conclusions hedge ('suggest', 'at least partially', 'suggestive evidence'). The flat statement in 4.2 Conclusions that violations 'are not associated with the development of dependence' should not be repeated in claims (Table 5: 1.6, 1.1 to 2.3; several intervals reach 1.0).

missed: Discussion, 6th paragraph, calls the number of early-onset mental disorders 'an important moderator of risk' for dependence. Table 5 enters them only as main-effect predictors, with no interaction terms, so 'moderator' is not supported. Claims should say 'predictor' or 'associated with'.

Definitions differ. Table 5 note 4 counts prescription drugs among the drug classes in the time-varying 'number of illicit drugs used' (cannabis, cocaine, prescription drugs or other drugs). Elsewhere 'other illicit drugs' excludes prescription drugs (Tables 2 to 5 notes). The 6.1, 15.4 and 35.7 odds ratios in key finding 5 therefore include non-medical prescription drug use as a class.

Minor reporting slip: the Table 1 note on sample design speaks of 'Nine of the 15 surveys' being nationally representative, while the paper pools 17 countries. The count matches neither the countries nor Table 1.

risk_of_bias.note: Some concerns is fair: two named databases, terms, dates, record counts and three screeners, but relevance as the only criterion and no appraisal. Overall equals the worst domain. For consistency: sc_mchugh_2018 rates its reuse of this search 'high', because databases and screening are not reported there.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is fair, but gap point (2) needs a correction. The Introduction does not call faster progression one of the most reproducible findings. That label goes to women's heightened vulnerability to adverse medical and social consequences; faster progression follows in the next sentence as an unlabelled statement of fact, which the paragraph later folds into 'this heightened vulnerability'. The same misreading appears in cl_gen_telescoping and in sc_keyes_2010's timeline entry for this review. The rest of point (2), Dawson (1996) pointing the other way, is confirmed.

missed: Section 5.2, 6th paragraph (Kaskutas et al. 2005): the women-only day programme did not differ from the two community-based mixed-gender programmes, and the authors conclude women may be equally well served by good mixed-gender and women-only day programmes. Key finding 12 gives only the hospital-programme difference.

Section 4.1, 5th paragraph (Satre 2004): after the abstinence difference disappeared with adjustment for length of stay, women still had no heavy-drinking days against an average of four in the past month for men.

Reporting issue, section 3.3, 2nd paragraph: the demonstration project (Roberts & Nishimoto 1996) is said to randomize women to a women-focused day programme or traditional outpatient care, but the completion comparison reported is against residential programmes. The description does not hang together and the finding should be taken from the primary paper.

key_findings_flagged.correction: The last clause should read: the unweighted associations with interpersonal problems and adult independence lost nominal significance after weighting. Interpersonal problems fell from 0.15 (SE 0.06) to 0.08 (0.08). Adult independence was essentially unchanged, 0.16 (0.07) to 0.15 (0.08), z about 1.9; it lost significance through a larger SE, not a smaller coefficient (for early intoxication 0.18 before and after weighting, Table 2B). 'Disappeared' overstates this.

The authors' reading of larger DZ estimates as partial genetic confounding is in the Discussion's 5th paragraph, not the 4th (8 paragraphs, checked in the page DOM). Results › Estimated Effects, 2nd paragraph, and Tables 2A/2B are correct.

Exposure measurement error is in the Discussion's 4th paragraph. The inability to separate causal effects from confounders not shared by co-twins is in the 6th paragraph. The card gives the 3rd and 5th (8 paragraphs, checked in the page DOM).

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E some concerns overall, with no domain worse than some concerns. Confounding at some concerns is defensible: propensity weighting plus co-twin control, with the twin's own early substance use and other non-shared factors unaddressed.

interpretation_gap.note: The card's four gaps are all correct, but they add up to 'substantial', not 'minor'. The abstract's Findings say outcomes related to 'social functioning' stayed significant after weighting, but none of the four social-functioning outcomes did. Its Conclusions say early exposures predict adult alcohol problems despite stringent adjustment for non-measured confounding, which failed in the cleanest test (MZ 0.17, SE 0.14) and for intoxication in all pairs (0.29, SE 0.15). The Discussion extends causal language to 'adult functioning'. The hedged final paragraph does not reach the abstract. This is a rating difference for the senior author.

missed: Abstract › Findings: after propensity weighting, 'several adult outcomes related to substance use or social functioning' remained significant. In Table 2A none of the four outcomes the Results call social functioning or independence (family relationships, interpersonal problems, social engagement, adult independence) did; only antisocial symptoms and dependent stressful life events, which the Results class separately, did.

Discussion, 2nd paragraph: the authors put the loss of significance for adult independence after weighting down to confounding, but the coefficient hardly changed (0.16 to 0.15; 0.18 to 0.18 for intoxication). The weighting widened the SE rather than removing an association. This affects key finding 2 and the card's 'results_show' sentence ('associations with social functioning and independence disappeared after weighting').

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E some concerns overall; domain judgments reasonable for the familial odds ratios. The risk-index and interaction results are weaker, as the reasoning says.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is defensible because the abstract's Results report the numbers faithfully; it is close to substantial, since the 'genetic' index includes biological parents' education, divorce and maternal age, the abstract's 'more pathogenic' conclusion rests on a probability-scale interaction alone, and the Comment's 'rule out' of intrauterine effects has no test. All of this is already listed in the card's text.

missed: Known point settled: the paper gives no heritability or variance-component estimate anywhere (the word appears only in a cited title); the card's 'No heritability percentage is estimated' and cannot_establish are right.

design_detail says 'drug-related criminal convictions', broader than the outcome definition the card itself gives under outcomes (Crime Register codes 5011 and 5012; convictions only for trafficking or possession, or only alcohol-related, excluded). The claim repeats 'a drug-related conviction'.

'Born in Sweden' (sample.recruitment) and 'domestic Swedish adoptions' (selection_effects) are inferences from the requirement of register data on a biological parent; the paper does not say so in words.

Minor inconsistencies: Table 4 prints the biological parents' univariate OR as 2.09 (1.66-2.63) against 1.66-2.62 in the abstract and Results; 'at least 70.9%' living with adoptive parents by age 5 does not match the age-5 cohort of 12,783 of 18,115 (70.6%).

key_findings_flagged.correction: The authors do not attribute the narrowing gap to weaker social restraints. They say the convergence is consistent with the possibility that protective social factors have diminished, list supporting research, and note that no formal test exists (Discussion, 4th paragraph). Write 'suggest, as a possibility', not 'attribute'. The recommendations (7th paragraph) are confirmed.

risk_of_bias.note: JBI prevalence suits a descriptive analysis of two probability surveys, and the partial-yes items are documented. Moderate is fair: good frames and response rates, against recalled timing, an estimand that is not the speed among those who reach each step, inconsistent denominators and an unclear age adjustment.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial is fair: the abstract's new claim rests on 'data not shown', and the Discussion's summary goes beyond Table 1. Point (1) of the gap is the editors' inference. It is well founded on Table 1 (23.7% of men vs 16.2% of women who drank became dependent, unweighted), but when the claim uses it, the claim should label it as the editors' reading and report the authors' opposite reading.

risk_of_bias.note: SYRCLE overall high (editors' summary). Item 1 'high' is justified by the fixed ascending order of the within-animal tests (dose, delay, cost; no fluid, water, saccharin), which the Methods and the Figure 2 legend state; between-group allocation alone would be 'unclear'. Item 8 'high' is right given outcome-related, uneven exclusion. Animal findings are labelled as such throughout, and doses appear only as study conditions, with no human-equivalent dose.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: 'clearly demonstrate' and 'drug-sensitized and -addicted individuals' rest on escalated intake alone. The human extensions (supernormal stimuli; sugar as a 'shield' against drug addiction) are speculation.

missed: Internal inconsistency: Results, 3rd paragraph, says the both-rewarded rats acquired the saccharin preference as quickly as the saccharin-only rats. Discussion, 5th paragraph, says they did so more rapidly (significant from day 2 vs day 7) and puts this down to cocaine's ambivalent effects. Minor.

Design detail: sampling always ran cocaine lever first (C-S-C-S), chosen to prevent drug-induced taste aversion (Materials and Methods › Discrete-trials choice procedure), so each saccharin sample followed a cocaine infusion. The fixed order is part of the procedure the result is tied to.
Results, 6th paragraph: 'This increase was not sufficient' refers to the decrease in saccharin choice with delay. A wording slip with no effect on the finding.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 critically low: several critical items not met (no protocol, PubMed only, no list of exclusions, no appraisal, no publication-bias assessment). The item 5 note is borne out by the Contributors statement in the collapsed Author information: one author ran the epidemiology search and the meta-analysis.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial, for the abstract's bare pooled figures, the untested alcohol-vs-cannabis comparison, the causal reading of cross-sectional imaging, and the unequal human-vs-animal counting. One correction to the card's reasoning: the review's statement that combined alcohol increases the reinforcing qualities of dopamine agonists is not contradicted by its cited monkey studies. It draws on the nomifensine increase and Czoty's concurrent-access phase (see key finding 10). It remains a generalization from a handful of monkeys.

missed: 3.3, 1st paragraph: in most of the 40 imaging studies, alcohol or cannabis dependence was an exclusion criterion for the control subjects only, so the cocaine groups and their controls differed in alcohol and cannabis dependence. This strengthens the point that imaging findings may mix effects.
3.3, 1st paragraph: the authors add that excluding polysubstance use is valid for some animal experiments; their point is that it is rarely considered.
Editors' reconstruction of the pooled estimates from Table 1 (see reporting issue 0): two of four reproduce exactly; the inputs to simultaneous alcohol and concurrent cannabis cannot be identified.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 critically low: two critical items clearly not met (item 2, no protocol; item 7, no list of excluded studies). The overall rating does not depend on the strict reading of item 4. Items 5 and 6 (no single-reviewer abstract screening; no stated duplicate extraction) and item 9 partial yes (narrative appraisal, no tool) agree with my reading.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the abstract's 'markedly attenuates or eliminates' and its policy recommendation go beyond four small cohorts, one of which showed an association unchanged by adjustment. The final paragraph also misclassifies that report.

missed: Rutgers odds ratios: both 2.39 and 5.75 are against a first drink at 11 or older at a family gathering (Table 1). The card and the claim give the place of the first drink but not the reference group.

Table 1 (Guttmannova 2011) also gives any-dependence ORs of 1.49, 1.16 and 0.35 and misuse-chronicity ORs of 1.20, 1.13 and 0.77, all p>0.05. The claim's magnitude should give the dependence ORs or stop attaching the misuse ORs to dependence.

key_findings_flagged.correction: Change 'who named telescoping' to 'widely credited with defining the term telescoping'. The paper says Lisansky first used 'telescoped development' in 1958 (key finding 1), so the 1989 paper did not coin the idea. All numbers confirmed: 33 women and 105 men; first drink about 2 and first intoxication about 3 years later; same age at treatment entry; 4.3 years.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist; high overall follows from the high search domain.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor: the conclusions are normative and presented as such.

missed: Khan et al. (2013), described as a national sample of 1,217 women and 3,297 men, is a NESARC analysis by its reference title, so it is a general-population study reported second-hand as finding the time to cannabis use disorder 2.5 years shorter in women. The card's results_show and where_it_stands present the general-population evidence as negative (Keyes et al., 2010) and should add this study, with its timing measure and adjustment unknown.

key_findings_flagged.correction: Delete 'oral': the review gives the THC doses (5 mg and 15 mg) without a route. The rest is confirmed; the doses stay study conditions only.

Only the past-month use figures (4.7%, 13.9%, 9.3%, 21.7%) are NSDUH. The 3.6% with alcohol use disorder and 1.6% with a drug use disorder are cited to Vesga-Lopez et al. (2008), a NESARC analysis by its reference title. The 8.7% is cited to Terplan et al. (2012) and the 6.8% of facilities offering childcare to SAMHSA (2017).

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist; high overall follows from unsystematic selection.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is fair. The abstract's summary that outcomes do not substantively differ omits the pharmacotherapy differences the review itself reports, most of which go against women. That is close to the review's own 'exception' framing and does not change the rating.

missed: Treatment Outcome, 3rd and 4th paragraphs: besides smoking cessation in general, the review reports nicotine replacement working better in men (Perkins & Scott 2008), poorer response in women to disulfiram for cocaine dependence (DeVito 2014), worse outcomes in women with buspirone for cannabis and cocaine dependence (no drug–placebo difference in either sex), and mixed naltrexone findings for alcohol (men better under some dosing). Varenicline relative to other aids is the one difference favouring women. Key finding 12 should record these: they bear directly on the claim that differences more often favoured women.

Gender-Specific and Gender-Responsive Treatments, 4th paragraph: randomized trials are cited as supporting gender-specific treatment for women with children, women with co-occurring disorders and women in the criminal justice system. Key finding 14 covers only the programme comparisons and the Women's Recovery Group.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 some concerns overall: per-protocol exclusions on manipulation checks and questionnaire wording that differs between the RQ1 arms; randomization, missing data and reporting low.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor. One nuance: results_show says 'no reliable effect of any factor on rewards or punishments', echoing the authors' Discussion (5th paragraph), but the drug-use description went with more money taken (62.05 vs 53.96 pence, p = .005, d .14, interval .02-.26), a small difference that could not be shown to be trivial or meaningful.

missed: The paper calls the 36.5% aged 18-25 'the majority'; it is the largest group, not a majority (the card already says 'largest age band').

The paper says all Stigma and Attribution Assessment subscales had acceptable reliability (alpha > .70) in this sample, but one printed alpha is .69 (besides the card's point that only four alphas are printed for five subscales).

can_establish and the claim say 'without personal or family experience of substance use or psychiatric diagnoses', which can be read as excluding anyone who had used drugs; the self-confirmed exclusion was of a substance use or psychiatric diagnosis in oneself or a known close relative.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, overall high: no search, no appraisal, no figures, dopamine emphasis beyond the body's evidence.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the abstract and Conclusions give dopamine genes a primacy that the reviewed genome-wide results do not show. The gap does not affect the claim, which uses only the twin summary, the replication point, the under-1% polygenic scores and the gene-environment examples.

missed: CORRECTION (known point settled), replication.timeline 2012 entry and replication.where_it_stands: they present Kendler et al. (2012) as 'a quantitative estimate with its population and era' and as an example of where heritability figures come from. Kendler et al. (2012) estimates no heritability (it gives rates and odds ratios of drug abuse in biological and adoptive relatives, risk-index odds ratios and a probability-scale interaction), and sc_kendler_2012 correctly records none. Prom-Wormley et al. (2017) does not cite Kendler et al. (2012) anywhere in its text or reference list (its 2012 Kendler citations are Dick & Kendler, 2012a/b), so the entry is an editors' cross-reference and should say so: 'National Swedish adoption study of registered drug abuse (Kendler et al., 2012): odds ratios in biological and adoptive relatives, no heritability estimate; not cited by this review'. where_it_stands should not name it as a source of heritability figures.

The section 3.1 twin summary that the claim uses (shared environment no longer significant for regular use or dependence in adulthood) cites Maes et al. (2017, Nicotine Tob Res 19:401-409), a twin-consortium paper co-authored by Prom-Wormley and Dick, whose reference entry lacks a title. The 'reliance on the authors' own studies' domain should name it alongside Prom-Wormley et al. (2015) and Dick & Kendler (2012).

reporting_issues_flagged.note: The sentence on 'the discussed paper's Fig. 3' ends 3.4.4 Drug abuse and (anti)social behavior, 6th paragraph (the paragraph on Moffitt, 1993). It is not in the last paragraph of 3.4.4 (the 13th). The issue itself is right: the paper has only one figure.

risk_of_bias.note: The editors' narrative-review checklist and overall high fit the paper. One count to correct: 29 of the 145 references (20%) include one of the 13 authors (my surname count over the full entries; Kreek and Bierut appear in none), not 30. The domain note and sample.n_by_group should say 29; 'about a fifth' is still right. I confirmed that Lynskey et al. (2003) and Fergusson et al. (2006) are not in the reference list.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' fits: 'empirically proven' (4. Conclusions) and 'readily refuted' (2. Gateway hypothesis, 3rd paragraph) overstate correlational and logical arguments, and the review treats the two explanations as mutually exclusive.

missed: Animal label. The only data the review cites against cannabis sensitization (3.2.2, 6th paragraph) is Ellgren, Hurd and Franck (2004). Its reference-list title shows a study of amphetamine effects after adolescent cannabinoid exposure, an animal study. Any use of this point must label it as animal evidence cited second-hand.

Women and men. The review cites an association of AVPR1A polymorphisms with addiction risk in men but not in women (Maher et al., 2011, with co-author Maher), reported as mediated by indicators of relationship quality (3.3 Sources of common variance, 7th paragraph). This is a single cited study and only a pointer, but the card does not record it.

Hicks et al. (2007): when the review cites this study again, it limits the growth in heritability with age to males ('at least in males', 3.4.4, 4th paragraph). Key finding 5 should carry that qualifier, and no population or era is given.

A cited figure is missing from analysis.effect_sizes: 'more than 50%' of people with addiction have other psychopathology (Regier et al., 1990, ECA), at 3.4.4, 8th paragraph. The source calls them 'addicts', so person-first wording is needed if it is reused.

reporting_issues_flagged.note: The issue is right: 0.02 and 0.03 are three-way interaction terms. The point estimates are right (0.22 x 4.56 x 9.56 x 0.02 = 0.19; 0.84 x 2.14 x 1.90 x 0.03 = 0.10). Two corrections. (1) Rounding range: about 0.14 to 0.25 (not 0.24) for parenthood and 0.08 (not 0.09) to 0.12 for a new job. (2) The consequence 'about ten times weaker' holds only for parenthood (0.19 vs 0.02, 9.6 times). For a new job, 0.10 vs 0.03 is about 3.4 times.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E is high overall, driven by confounding, for the life-transition associations. The descriptive decomposition is reasonably separated in the reasoning. I agree with the domain judgments.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Minor' is defensible because the abstract hedges ('tended to', 'not dramatically') and the decomposition headline follows from the results. However, the Results misread the interaction terms by a large factor. Any claim on parenthood or employment and persistence must use the card's reporting issues 0 to 1, not the paper's text.

missed: Robustness of the persistence three-way interactions differs by check. With multiple imputation, only the parenthood interaction stayed significant (Results > Role Transitions..., 3rd paragraph). With persistence redefined as AD at Wave 1 plus at least one symptom at Wave 2, only the job three-way interaction was significant (Results > Alternative Definitions of Persistence and Recurrence, 1st paragraph). With a continuous-diagnosis definition, only the parenthood interaction remained (2nd paragraph). Neither interaction survives every check; key findings 5 and 7 should say so.

New onset and recurrence count only dependence present in the 12 months before Wave 2. Dependence that began or recurred and then remitted earlier in the roughly three-year interval is not counted, so it falls into the 'consistent non-diagnosis' or 'non-recurrent' groups. The 2.5% and 8.8% in key finding 4 are therefore past-year statuses at follow-up among the people at risk, not three-year cumulative incidences, and they understate onsets and recurrences over the interval. The authors call their approach 'time-sampling' (Results > Alternative Definitions..., 2nd paragraph).
